transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. Can you start by telling me what's been bringing you in to see me?

Yeah, um… I guess the main thing is work. I’m a claims clerk, and I’m supposed to stay at my workstation and get through claim reviews, but I keep finding myself getting up during the day. Like, not for anything that important necessarily, just… stepping away when I know I should be sitting there finishing things.

It’s not like I’m trying to cause problems or anything, and I do want to do my job well. It just keeps happening enough that I figured I should probably talk to someone about it, if that makes sense.
Have you noticed this kind of restlessness or trouble staying seated and focused going back to when you were a child or teenager, or is this something that's really only started more recently?

Yeah, I think… looking back, it probably isn’t totally new. I don’t want to make it sound like I was a terrible student or anything—I was usually considered pretty bright, I think—but in elementary school teachers would write things like I lost worksheets, or I missed instructions, or I needed reminders to finish classwork.

So, I guess some version of it was there earlier. Does that count as the kind of thing you mean?
Do you notice this same kind of restlessness or trouble focusing in other areas of your life—like at home, during conversations, or with hobbies—or does it really only happen at work?

I’m not totally sure, honestly. Work is where I notice it the most because there are expectations and people can kind of see if I’m not staying on task.

At home… I mean, maybe a little, but I don’t know if it’s the same thing or just normal distraction. I haven’t really tracked it. In conversations I try pretty hard to pay attention, so I’d like to think it’s not too noticeable. Does that answer what you’re asking?
Can you give me a specific example of a time recently when this restlessness or trouble focusing caused a problem at home—like leaving a task unfinished or forgetting something important?

Um… at home specifically, I’m trying to think of a good example. I notice it more with work things that kind of follow me in my head after I leave, if that counts.

Like, I’ll mean to return a claimant’s call, or update a diary note, or send a form before the end of the day, and then I realize later I didn’t do it. It’s usually not some huge disaster, but it’s embarrassing because it’s simple stuff I really did intend to follow up on. I don’t know if that’s the kind of example you mean.

Can you think of a specific recent example at home—like paying a bill, doing a chore, or managing a personal task—where you started it but got distracted and didn't finish, similar to what happens at work?

Yeah… I’m trying to think of a clean example. At home it’s more like if I’m reading something—like a form or something I need to deal with—and then someone near me starts talking about another claim, or I suddenly remember some random errand, my attention kind of slides off.

Then I realize I’ve been looking at the same paragraph but not taking it in, so I have to reread the same section a few times. It feels a little silly because it’s not like I’m choosing to stop, I just sort of lose the thread. Is that the kind of thing you mean?

Do you often feel physically restless—like fidgeting, needing to get up, or feeling like you have to be moving—even in situations outside of work, such as sitting through a movie or a long conversation?

Yeah, I mean… not in a really dramatic way, I don’t think. But in trainings or longer team meetings, I do catch myself bouncing my leg or clicking my pen, or just shifting around in the chair a lot.

I’m usually trying to look like I’m paying attention, so I don’t know how noticeable it is to other people. It’s more like I feel a little uncomfortable sitting completely still for that long. Does that count as what you mean?
Have people close to you—like family or friends—ever commented on you seeming distracted, restless, or forgetful outside of work, even before you had this job?

Yeah… I guess looking back, it wasn’t totally new with this job. I don’t know how much this matters, but in elementary school, teachers would write things like I was bright, but I’d lose worksheets or miss instructions, and I needed reminders to finish classwork.

At the time it was kind of framed like I just needed to be more organized or try harder, so I don’t want to make it sound worse than it was. But yes, there were comments like that before.

Aside from work, has this pattern of losing focus or restlessness ever caused a real problem at home—like forgetting to pay a bill, missing an appointment, or upsetting a family member because you didn't finish something you said you would?

Um… outside of work, I’m not sure I have a really solid example like a bill or appointment that I can point to.

The more concrete problem has honestly been at work. My supervisor put me on performance coaching because my claim files are getting behind, and they’ve been questioning my accuracy. I’m trying not to make it sound dramatic, but it does worry me because I was aiming for the senior adjuster track, and now I’m kind of scared I could lose that chance. Is that still relevant to what you’re asking?

Do you notice this same kind of losing focus or restlessness during things you actually enjoy and choose to do, like a hobby, a book, or a game—something with no work pressure attached—or does it really only show up when there's stress or deadlines involved?

Yeah… I think it’s not only deadlines, but it’s definitely easier to notice then.

Even when I’m reading something I chose to read, or doing something that’s supposed to be interesting, if people near me start talking about another claim or I suddenly remember some random errand I need to do, my attention kind of slips off. Then I realize I’ve been looking at the same paragraph and didn’t really take it in, so I have to reread it a few times.

It’s not like I can never focus on enjoyable things, so I don’t want to overstate it. But that “attention sliding away” thing does happen outside of pressure too, if that’s what you mean.
Do you notice yourself frequently interrupting others, blurting out responses before someone finishes speaking, or having trouble waiting your turn—whether at work, at home, or in social situations?

Not really, I don’t think so. I mean, I might accidentally talk over someone once in a while like anyone does, but I wouldn’t say people complain that I interrupt a lot or that I can’t wait my turn.

If anything, I’m usually trying pretty hard not to come across as rude, so I tend to hold back. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Before this job, did you notice similar problems with focus or restlessness causing difficulties in other jobs, or in college/training programs you attended?

Yeah… looking back, I guess it wasn’t completely new with this job. I don’t want to make it sound like I was a “problem kid” or anything, because I did okay in some ways, but in elementary school teachers would write things like that I was bright, but I lost worksheets, missed instructions, or needed reminders to finish my classwork.

I hadn’t really connected that to what’s happening now until you asked. Is that the kind of history you mean?

Before this job, can you think of a specific time in college or a previous job where this kind of distractibility or restlessness actually caused a concrete problem—like a missed deadline, a bad grade, or a warning from a supervisor?

I’m trying to think of a clean example, and honestly I’m not sure I can point to one specific incident like, “this exact thing happened and I got written up.”

In college, I remember having trouble keeping up with assignments and kind of scrambling at the last minute, but I don’t know if I’d call it a concrete disaster or anything. And in previous work, I don’t remember a formal warning. Maybe people reminded me about things, but… I’m not sure that counts?

Sorry, I don’t want to force an example if I can’t remember it clearly.
Outside of work, do you often misplace everyday things like your keys, wallet, or phone, or forget personal appointments or errands you'd planned to do?

Yeah… I mean, I don’t want to overstate it, but I do spend a lot of time looking for things I just had.

At work especially, I’ll put down a claim form, or my headset, or a sticky note with someone’s callback number, and then a few minutes later I’m searching around like, “Where did I put that?” Same with my access badge sometimes. It’s embarrassing because it feels like it should be simple.

Outside of work it happens too, but I guess the work examples stand out more. Is that the kind of thing you’re asking about?

Can you think of a specific time outside of work when losing focus or forgetfulness actually caused a real consequence—like a late fee from a missed bill, a missed personal appointment, or a friend or family member being upset because you forgot something important?

I’m trying to think of outside work, and I don’t know if I have a really clear example like a missed appointment or a late fee.

The thing I can say for sure is more at work, honestly… I forget simple follow-ups more than I’d like to admit. Like I’ll mean to return a claimant’s call, or update a diary note, or send a form before the end of the day, and then I realize later I didn’t do it. It’s not usually because I don’t care, I just… lose track of it.

I know that’s not exactly outside of work like you asked, but that’s the most concrete example I can think of. Is that still useful?
Has a spouse, partner, or close friend ever told you they felt hurt, ignored, or frustrated because you seemed distracted or forgot something that mattered to them?

Not really in a clear way, I guess. I mean, I’m sure people close to me have been annoyed with me before, but I can’t think of a specific time where someone said they felt hurt because I forgot something important.

The clearest thing I can point to is still more work-related. I do forget simple follow-ups more than I’d like to admit—like returning a claimant’s call, updating a diary note, or sending a form I meant to send earlier that day. I know that’s not exactly the personal-relationship example you’re asking for, but that’s where it shows up most clearly for me. Is that okay to mention?

Is there a specific household responsibility you're in charge of—like managing bills, cooking, or a regular chore—where your distractibility has caused a real problem, such as a late payment, burnt food, or something not getting done on time?

I don’t think I have a good example at home, like a late bill or burning food or something like that.

The pattern I’m more sure of is at work, honestly. I’ll mean to do a simple follow-up—return a claimant’s call, update a diary note, send a form I’d planned to send before the end of the day—and then later I realize I just didn’t do it. It’s not usually some huge disaster, but it happens more than I’d like to admit.

Sorry, I know you’re asking specifically about household stuff. That’s just the clearest version I can point to.
Have you ever gotten into a driving problem—like missing your exit, forgetting where you parked, or nearly missing a turn—because your attention drifted while driving?

Not really with driving, no—not that I can think of. I mean, I’ve maybe missed a turn here or there like anyone does, but I don’t have a strong example where it caused a real problem.

The attention drifting thing happens more when I’m reading something, especially at work. Like if people near me start talking about another claim, or I suddenly remember some random errand, my attention kind of slides off what I’m reading. Then I realize I didn’t absorb any of it and I have to reread the same section a few times.

I know that’s not exactly driving, but that’s the closest version of it that I can describe clearly.

Thinking about personal projects or hobbies you care about—like a home improvement task, a craft, or a personal goal—have you ever left one unfinished or fallen behind on it because your attention drifted, even without any work pressure involved?

I’m not sure I have a strong personal-project example, honestly. I don’t want to make one up.

It’s more obvious for me when I’m reading at work. If people near me start talking about another claim, or I suddenly remember some random errand I need to do, my attention just kind of slips off what I’m reading. Then I realize I got through the paragraph but didn’t actually take it in, so I have to go back and reread it, sometimes more than once.

So with hobbies or home projects, I can’t think of a clear unfinished one because of that, but that “getting pulled off track” thing definitely happens. Does that answer what you mean?
Was your attention or restlessness ever formally evaluated by a doctor, school counselor, or psychologist when you were a child, or has anyone ever suggested you might have ADHD before now?

I don’t think I was ever formally evaluated as a kid, at least not that I know of.

But looking back, it wasn’t completely new, I guess. In elementary school, teachers would write things like I was bright, but I’d lose worksheets, miss instructions, or need reminders to finish classwork. At the time I think everyone just treated it like I was kind of careless or not paying close enough attention.

I don’t remember anyone specifically saying this might be ADHD back then, though. Does that kind of school feedback count for what you’re asking?

On days when you're completely away from work—like a weekend with no work on your mind at all—do you still notice that same restlessness or trouble focusing, or does it mostly ease up when you're not thinking about your job?

It mostly eases up when I’m not dealing with work reading, I think. I don’t want to overstate it.

The clearest place I notice it is still at work—like when I’m reading a claim and people near me start talking about another one, or I suddenly remember some random errand. My attention just kind of drifts off the page, and then I realize I didn’t actually take in what I read, so I have to reread the same section a few times.

On a weekend, if I’m not reading something like that or trying to focus in the same way, I might not notice it as much. Is that the kind of difference you mean?

doctor.intent: Identify the primary reason for the visit today
doctor.question: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. Can you start by telling me what's been bringing you in to see me?

target_item.name: Leaving_Seat
target_item.manifestation: The main thing that pushed me to come in is that I keep getting up from my workstation during the day, even when I know I’m supposed to stay put and finish my claim reviews.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so I’m returning the chief complaint symptom code as instructed.

patient.answer:
Yeah, um… I guess the main thing is work. I’m a claims clerk, and I’m supposed to stay at my workstation and get through claim reviews, but I keep finding myself getting up during the day. Like, not for anything that important necessarily, just… stepping away when I know I should be sitting there finishing things.

It’s not like I’m trying to cause problems or anything, and I do want to do my job well. It just keeps happening enough that I figured I should probably talk to someone about it, if that makes sense.

inference.note: Initial presentation of difficulty sustaining task focus/staying seated at work; broad differential includes ADHD (inattentive/combined), anxiety, depressive disorder, or a personality/behavioral pattern, as well as nonclinical occupational stress. Further history needed on duration, onset (childhood vs adult), mood, anxiety symptoms, and functional impact.

doctor.intent: Determine whether this pattern of restlessness/difficulty staying seated has been present since childhood or is a recent change, to help distinguish ADHD from other causes
doctor.question: Have you noticed this kind of restlessness or trouble staying seated and focused going back to when you were a child or teenager, or is this something that's really only started more recently?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Looking back, this wasn’t brand new for me; in elementary school my teachers used to write that I was bright but lost worksheets, missed instructions, and needed reminders to finish classwork.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether these problems go back to childhood or started recently, which directly relates to onset before age 12.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I think… looking back, it probably isn’t totally new.
